text:
Verses 84-90

In the name of Allah, the most Merciful, the most Compassionate

(6:84) And We gave to him Isaac and Jacob; each did We guide, and Noah did We guide before, and of his descendants, David and Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses and Aaron; and thus do We reward the good-doers.

(6:85) And Zachariah, John, Jesus and Elias; every one was of the righteous;

(6:86) And Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah and Lot; and every one, We preferred them above the nations:

(6:87) And from among their fathers and their descendants and their brethren, and We chose them and guided them to a straight path.

(6:88) This is Allah’s guidance, He guides thereby whom He wills of His servants; and if they had associated others (with Him), certainly what they did would have become ineffectual for them.

(6:89) Those are they to whom We gave the book and the judgment and the prophethood; therefore if these disbelieve in it We have already entrusted with it a people who are not disbelievers in it.

(6:90) These are they whom Allah guided, therefore follow their guidance. Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it; it is nothing but

a reminder to the nations.

Introduction

The connection between these verses and the previous verses is clear and without need of explanation, because here Abraham’s story continues. These verses describe some of God’s favors upon him and upon some

other prophets who are named with him, as He says: And We gave to him Isaac and Jacob (6:84); And thus do We reward the good-doers (6:84); And every one We preferred them above the nations (6:86), and other verses. However, unlike what some exegetes have said, this is not the only purpose of these verses. Rather, these favors are mentioned as the great blessings and pleasant graces that ensue from accepting God’s guidance and

following the innate monotheism which is embedded in human nature. This complies better with the theme of the entire chapter, which is to clarify tawḥīd (monotheism, God’s oneness) in a way that it conforms to the innate human nature and disposition (fiṭrah). As we said, Abraham’s story here is mentioned as an example of the general principles discussed in the previous part of the chapter.

In addition to explaining monotheism, these verses also indicate that God has always preserved monotheism among people through a continuous chain, with links that were connected by God’s guidance. Thus

God has prevented humankind’s divine innate nature from failing to actualize altogether due to satanic desires. Otherwise, the entire creation would be purposeless and pointless. God alludes to this [continuation] by expressions such as: And We gave to him…. (6:84); And Noah did We guide before, and of his descendants (6:84); And from among their fathers and their descendants and their brethren (6:87 therefore if these disbelieve in it… (6:89). These verses also outline the distinguishing points between divine guidance and other ways, including:

(1) Being chosen [by God];

(2) Having a straight path;

(3) Being given a book;

(4) Being given judgment; and

(5) Being given prophethood.

We shall discuss these below, by God’s will.

Commentary

(6:84) And We gave to him Isaac and Jacob; each (kullan) did We guide, and Noah did We guide before, and of his descendants, David and Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses and Aaron; and thus do We reward the good-doers.

Isaac was Abraham’s son, and Jacob was Isaac’s son. Exegetes have explained that the word kullan (each, every, all) in each did We guide is mentioned at the beginning of the phrase in order to indicate that each of them received divine guidance independently, as opposed to some of them receiving it independently—like Abraham—and others receiving it through him. This is equivalent to saying: “We guided Abraham, We guided Isaac, and We guided Jacob.”

… and Noah did We guide before…: This statement suggests that God’s guidance has always existed through a continuous chain. It is not something that began with Abraham, but before him this mercy had embraced Noah.

… and of his descendants, David and Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses and Aaron; and thus do We reward the good-doers (al-muḥsinīn, from iḥsān): As some exegetes have explained, the pronoun “his” in his descendants must refer to Noah because of two reasons: (1) that was the last name

mentioned; and (2) some of the people listed below were not Abraham’s descendants, such as Lot and Elias.

Others have said that the pronoun refers to Abraham, and Lot and Elias are mentioned alongside his descendants by generalization (taghlīb).1 A similar verse [where the pronoun refers to Abraham] is: And We granted

1 Taghlīb is when a mixed group is entirely described by the quality of some of them, even though that quality does not apply to all of them. (Trans.) him Isaac and Jacob, and caused the prophethood and the book to remain in his seed (29:27).

Another view is that the word “descendants” only includes the six prophets named in this verse [6:84], not the rest of the prophets mentioned in the next verses. The next two verses—And Zachariah… And Ishmael…

(6:85-86)—do not add to “David,” but they add to and of his descendants. However, this view does not match the context and flow of the verses.1 … and thus (kadhālika) do We reward the good-doers: Apparently the “reward” mentioned here is the above-mentioned divine guidance [where the verse says, each did We guide, and Noah did We guide before]. The word kadhālika is used to refer to something at a distance. Its usage here indicates the lofty status and magnificence of God’s guidance. It is similar to

its usage in the verse: Thus (kadhālika) does Allah set forth parables (13:17). The meaning is: “We reward the good-doers like this.”

(6:85) And Zachariah, John, Jesus and Elias; every one was of the righteous (al-ṣāliḥīn, from ṣalāḥ)

We have already discussed the meaning of iḥsān (excellent, gooddoing) and ṣalāḥ (righteousness).2 The verse also names Jesus as one of

the descendants of Noah even though his only connection is through his mother. This is a clear indication that the Noble Qur’an considers the children and descendants of one’s daughter to be part of one’s own children

and descendants. A similar conclusion was made before from verses on inheritance and unlawful marriages.3 We shall complete this discussion below under our examination of the narrations, by God’s will.

1 The apparent meaning is that all of the names listed in these verses are “of his descendants.” This means that the next two verses add to “David.” If they add to “and of his descendants,” then the meaning would be: “And We also guided Zachariah… and We also guided Ishmael…” (Trans.)

2 Iḥsān refers to the end of the last verse. The author has discussed iḥsān under

verses 2:195, 3:134 and 5:93; and ṣalāḥ under verses 2:130, 4:69 and 6:74. (Trans.)

3 These are verses 4:7, 4:11 and 4:23-24. The author has quoted and discussed them at the end of his discussion of the current set of verses. (Trans.)

(6:86) And Ishmael, Elisha (al-Yasaʿ), Jonah and Lot; and every one, We preferred them above the nations.

Apparently, “Ishmael” here refers to Abraham’s son and Isaac’s brother. Al-Yasaʿ is also pronounced as Al-Laysaʿ. He was apparently an Israelite prophet whom God has named next to Ishmael, as in the verse: And remember Ishmael and Elisha and Dhū al-Kif ; and they were all of the good

(38:48). However, the Qur’an does not discuss his story.

… and every one We preferred them above the nations (al-ʿālamīn): ʿĀlam is a group of people such as the ʿālam of the Arabs, the ʿālam of the Persians, and the ʿālam of the Romans [where ʿālam means “nation, world, community”]. Being preferred over the nations refers to their higher position compared to the people of their time in the sense that they were the first ones who directly received God’s special guidance, as opposed to others who were blessed with guidance through them. One can also say that they have been preferred over people of all times, not just their contemporaries, in the sense that they were guided by the divine guidance

embedded in the innate human nature without any intermediary. God’s direct guidance is a blessing that is an advantage for those who receive it over those who do not. This blessing has embraced the group mentioned here—including the prophets and those related to them like their fathers, descendants, and brethren. Thus this group is preferred above everyone else by God’s preference.

Overall, the criterion of this preference is benefiting from God’s direct guidance without any intermediary. The prophets are preferred over others because this applies to them. Now, if one can conceive of others who are also subject to this guidance—such as the angels, as one can infer from God’s words; and such as the Imams, as we mentioned under the verse: And when his Lord tried Abraham with certain words (2:124)—then the prophets would not be preferred above them in this aspect, although they could be preferred over them in aspects other than guidance. Given the above explanation, one cannot draw on this verse—as some exegetes have done—to show that the prophets are superior to the angels.

It should also be clear that their preference is only because of the special divine guidance which embraced them without any intermediary. The

preference mentioned in this verse is not based on their other qualities such as being chosen, being on the straight path, and having been given scripture, judgment and prophethood.

You should know that the seventeen prophets named in these three verses [6:84-86] are mentioned neither in chronological order, as is obvious, nor according to their rank. Noah, Moses and Jesus are mentioned

in the midst of them, even though they were superior to the rest of them according to the explicit text of the Qur’an, as we explained in our discussion on prophethood under verse 2:213.1

Here is a summary of the explanation offered by the author of al-Manār about the order of the fourteen2 prophets named in these verses: These prophets are grouped into three categories based on a commonality between them. The first group includes David, Solomon,

Job, Joseph, Moses and Aaron. The common quality between them is that in addition to being prophets and messengers, God made them kings, rulers, judges, and leaders in the community.

The verse first names David and Solomon, who were kings with wealth and affluence. Then it mentions Job and Joseph, where Job was a great, rich and benevolent ruler, and Joseph was a great vizier with authority. Both of them were tested by difficulty, where they showed patience; and they were also tested by ease, where they showed gratitude. The verse then names Moses and Aaron who were rulers among their people but were not kings.

Each of these three pairs shared a distinct quality. Their order is based on their enjoyment of worldly bounties, for David and Solomon were more materially endowed than Job and Joseph, who were in turn more materially endowed than Moses and Aaron. It could also be that the pairs escalate in terms of religious value, because apparently Moses and Aaron were superior to Job and Joseph, who were in turn superior to David and

Solomon because of incorporating both patience in difficulty and gratefulness in ease.

The second group includes Zachariah, John, Jesus and Elias. Their distinct quality was their high degree of zuhd (disinterestedness, aversion, renunciation) with regards to the pleasures and adornments this world (dunyā). That is why the verse describes them as

1 See volume 3 of the English translation, pp. 183ff. (Trans.)

2 Fourteen is if we start the count from David, excluding Isaac, Jacob and Noah.

(Trans.)

“the righteous” (al-ṣāliḥīn), for this quality fits them more when they are compared to others, even though all prophets were righteous and good-doers in the absolute sense.

The third group includes Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah and Lot. They are mentioned last because there is no unique quality that was common among them. They neither had kingdom and dominion in

this world, as in the case of the first group, nor an intense degree of aversion to this world, as in the case of the third group.

Al-Rāzī has a similar explanation in his Tafsīr, although al-Manār’s explanation is more plausible. The problem with both explanations, however, is that they consider the third group to be devoid of any distinct

quality. This is not true. As with Ishmael, God tested him with the trial of being slaughtered, and he was patient with God’s trial. God says: So We gave him [Abraham] the good news of a boy, possessing forbearance. And when he attained [the age of] working with him, he said: O my son! Surely I have seen in a dream that I should sacrifice you; consider then what you see. He said: O my father! Do what you are commanded; you will find me, if Allah wills, of the patient ones (37:101-102). This is an exalted characteristic by which God distinguished Ishmael, and a clear tribulation by

which he stands out, to the extent that God has made sacrifice as a universal requirement in hajj in order to remind everyone of the ordeal that

Ishmael endured in God’s way. This is how God made his remembrance last among the posterity. Moreover, he was the partner of his noble father in building the Kaʿbah, which is itself a sufficient distinction. As with Prophet Jonah, God tested him with a trial that He did not mete out to any other prophet. Jonah was swallowed by the fish, wherein he called out in the darkness: There is no god but Thou, glory be to Thee; surely I was among the wrongdoers (21:87).

As with Lot, the unique tribulations that he faced in God’s way are also mentioned in the Noble Qur’an. He faced the first difficulties of his life alongside Abraham, until when they migrated from their people and homeland. Then God sent him to the people of Sodom and its vicinity, who used to commit an indecency which was completely unprecedented in the world.1 They persisted with their evil practice until they were taken by God’s exterminating punishment. At that point, there was only one

1 See verses 7:80 and 29:28. (Trans.)

household that had submitted to God,1 and that was Lot’s household, with the exception of his wife.

As with Elisha (al-Yasaʿ), none of his story appears in the Qur’an. According to some narrations, he was the successor of Ilyās (Elias, Elijah).2 He went to his people with miracles similar to those of Jesus son of Mary, such as bringing the dead to life, and healing the blind and the epileptic. God tested his people with a massive famine and drought.

Hence, it is better to correct the above explanation about the order of the prophets who are named in these verses as follows.

The first group—which includes six prophets—consists of those who had kingdom and rule on top of messengership. The next four prophets are distinct for their disinterestedness from this world and their aversion to its adornments. The third group—which includes four prophets—consists of prophets with various distinction and great divine tests. Each of them were distinguished by a specific quality. And God knows best.

Another problem with the above explanation offered by the author of al-Manār is his point about the superiority of Moses and Aaron over Job and Joseph, and their superiority over David and Solomon. There is no evidence to support his view. The same applies to his interpretation of ṣalāḥ

(righteousness) as zuhd (material disinterestedness and renunciation).

(6:87) And from among their fathers and their descendants and their brethren, and We chose them and guided them to a straight path.

This verse confirms what we said above: that the purpose of these verses is to indicate the continuity of the chain of divine guidance. This is because the verse adds these groups to the previously mentioned individuals as their fathers, children or brothers.

… and We chose them (ijtabaynāhum, from ijtibāʾ) and guided them to a straight path: Al-Rāghib says in al-Mufradāt:

When one gathers and stores water in a pool he says: jabaytu al-māʾ. Jābiyah is the name of a pool where water gathers, and its

1 See verse 51:36. (Trans.)

2 See 1 Kings 19:16. (Trans.)

plural is jawāb. God says: and bowls (large) as watering-troughs (kal-jawāb) (34:13). The verb jabaytu is used metaphorically when one collects taxes. Another similar usage is found in the verse:

to which fruits of every kind shall be drawn (yujbá ilayhi) (28:57). Ijtibāʾ means “to gather by selection (iṣṭifāʾ).” God says [about Prophet Jonah]: Then his Lord chose him (ijtabāhu) (68:50)….

God’s ijtibāʾ (choosing, selection) is when He favors a servant with an exclusive divine grace which results in various bounties for the servant without any effort on his part. This applies to the prophets and others who are close to them, such as the truthful and the martyrs, as the Qur’an says [where Prophet Jacob tells his son Joesph]: And thus will your Lord choose you (yajtabīka) (12:6). Similarly, the Qur’an says: Then his Lord chose him (ijtabāhu), and He made him of the righteous (68:50); And We chose them (ijtabaynāhum) and guided them to a straight path (6:87); Then his [Adam’s] Lord chose him (ijtabāhu), so He turned to him and guided (him) (20:122); He chooses (yajtabī) for Himself whom He wills, and guides to Himself him who turns (to Him), frequently

(42:13).

Al-Rāghib’s definition is consistent with the usage of ijtibāʾ in the Qur’an. However, this is not the original meaning of the term, but an implication and consequence of it, which pertains to God’s treatment of His chosen servants. The theme of these verses suggests that what is intended here is the root meaning of the term, which is “to gather things from various places and dispersed positions.” This would set the grounds for the next part of the verse, which talks about their guidance to the straight path. It is as if God is saying: “We gathered them despite their original dispersion. Then, when they all gathered and joined one another, We guided them all to such-and-such a path….”

This interpretation is according to the theme and purpose of these verses, which, as we discussed above, is to explain the continuity of the chain of those who have been guided by the divine guidance embedded in the innate human nature. To convey this meaning, it is most befitting to imagine them as gathered and united, such that divine mercy would embrace them as one unit, where they follow a single form of guidance, and that leads them to a single straight path which is free from any discrepancy whatsoever. They all follow the same path that is consistent in

terms of:

(a) Its time and circumstances;

(b) Its parts and components;

(c) Its callers and followers; and

(d) Its goal and destination.1

The path to which they are guided may differ in terms of wideness and narrowness of their apparent laws, but these laws differ only in terms of concision and elaboration, as per the capacity of different nations. Nonetheless, they are all unanimous over a single reality which is innately embedded in human nature: God’s oneness and the necessity of serving Him alone. The whole human formation is designed by God in such a way that inherently points to monotheism. Clearly there is no transformation or alteration of the creation and formation of the human being in and of itself, such that it would change the principles of human cognition and voluntary motion. The senses in the outside, the emotions and feelings in the inside, and the center of decision making and judgment—which is the innate power of reason—ever follow a fixed and unchanging set of principles throughout all human beings, even though specific views and goals for humanity may eventually evolve since they pertain to the requirements of life in every age and time.

Humans always feel a need for food, drink, clothes, shelter and sex. They always crave things that give comfort to their covetous souls, and dislike what harms and hurts them. They constantly want a happy life, and are afraid of misery and an evil end. These inclinations are always present in humankind, even though the appearance of their life and activities may change from time to time and from one generation to another. God says: Then set your face upright for the religion purely—the nature made by Allah in which He has made men; there is no altering of Allah’s creation; that is the right religion, but most people do not know (30:30). The pure divine religion that upholds human society is what the innate human nature calls to and what the human creation inclines toward. This innate calling and inclination is based on the existential needs of human nature. Our souls are inspired with the means of our felicity in terms of right beliefs and actions—that is, in terms of facts, ethics and rituals. This is something that never undergoes any change or replacement because it is based on a

1 The author has explained each of these below. (Trans.)

fixed nature and creation. Thus it should be clear that:

(a) The innate human nature’s call to human felicity [that is, the innate religious call] is not limited to any specific time or circumstance. (b) The innate religious call is also free from any discrepancy within its parts, meaning that no part of the pure religion opposes or contradicts another part of it, and there is nothing in it that necessitates an inner invalidation of it. This is because all parts of religion are nurtured from the same breast of monotheism (tawḥīd), and this gives religion the best balance. They are like our physical faculties and organs: if they come in conflict with one another or one part transgresses over another, then they will be checked and set in place by a supervising faculty that regulates each part according to its significance and impact in stabilizing human life. (c) The divine innate religion does not differ from person to person. That is, those who are guided by this guidance follow the same course. None of these leaders calls the people to something different than another caller, even though their calls differ in terms of elaboration and concision, according to the evolution of human societies over time. God says: Surely the (only) religion with Allah is Islam (3:19); He has made plain to you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We have revealed to you, and that which We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus: that maintain the religion and be not divided therein (42:13).

(d) This religion is also consistent and uniform in terms of its goal and objective, both of which lie in monotheism, which is the point of reference of all religious beliefs, moral values, and legal injunctions. God says: Surely this is your nation, one nation (only), and I am your Lord; therefore serve Me (21:92); And We did not send before you any messenger but We revealed to him that there is no god but Me; therefore serve Me(21:25).

The above should clarify the meaning of His words: and We chose them and guided them to a straight path (ṣirāṭan mustaqīman) (6:87). The word ṣirāṭ (path) is indefinite in terms of infiection, as opposed to its definite usage in other verses like: Guide us to the straight path (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm). The path of those upon whom Thou hast blessed (1:6-7). The use of indefinite here directs the mind to the attribute of the path: straightness (istiqāmah). If something is straight, it means that it is uniform and

consistent in terms of its qualities and specifications. This shows that they were guided to a path that was devoid of any discrepancy in any way and aspect. This can only make sense because it is about a path based on the innate human nature, which is how the human being has been created and fashioned. This basic formation and creation of humankind does not change in terms of its guidance and direction toward the existential goals of the human species.

Those who are guided to this straight path are under God’s security from the dangers of the journey and the slips of the way. This is because they are treading a way that does not vary in terms of guidance and misguidance, truth and falsehood, and felicity and wretchedness. Rather,

its parts are all consistent and uniform at all times. It is a path that is founded on the truth and leads to the truth. It does not leave its follower in confusion, nor does it take the person to iniquity, disobedience and wretchedness. God says: Those who believe and do not mix up their belief with iniquity, those are they who shall have the security and they are those who have found guidance (6:82).

(6:88) This is Allah’s guidance, He guides thereby whom He wills of His servants; and if they had associated others (with Him), certainly what they did would have become ineffectual for them.

Here God defines His special guidance by which He guides whomever He wills among His servants. It was through this divine grace that He guided the above-mentioned prophets. True guidance is only that which comes from God. We can verify whether one is blessed with God’s guidance if: (1) the person is on the path of other guided individuals, which

are the noble prophets of God; and (2) the person’s path is composed of a consistent set of components which all revolve around monotheism, promote the call of truth, and bear the mark of servitude and taqwá (Godwariness, self-restraint, piety).

On the other hand there are some paths that differentiate between God’s messengers by accepting some and rejecting others, or differentiate between God’s laws and orders by taking some and leaving out others.

There are also paths that do not secure a felicitous life for human society, but result in unfavorable outcomes. God is by no means pleased with such paths, for they deviate from humankind’s innate nature and makeup, to the pitfalls of misguidance and slippery footholds of desires. Being guided by these paths is not God’s guidance.

The Qur’an says: Surely those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and (those who) desire to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers and say: We believe in some and disbelieve in others, and desire to

take a course between (this and) that. These it is that are truly disbelievers, and We have prepared for the disbelievers a disgraceful chastisement (4:150- 151); Do you then believe in a part of the Book and disbelieve in the other? What then is the re ward of such among you as do this but disgrace in the life of this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they shall be sent back to the most grievous chastisement (2:85); And who is more erring than he who follows his low desires without any guidance from Allah? Surely Allah does not guide the unjust people (28:50). What is meant here is that a path which involves the following of desires is nothing but error and misguidance; it does not lead its traveler to a felicitous life. This is not God’s guidance because it consists of injustice, while God has never decreed injustice, has not made it a means to happiness. One can by no means achieve happiness through wrongdoing.

In short, the special feature of God’s guidance is that it is completely free from misguidance and does not lead to any form of error. It is sheer guidance that brings about sheer happiness as an unending gif . Meanwhile, God’s bestowal is not like the gifts that are common among us, where the gifiileaves the hand of the giver upon its conferment, and the ownership transfers to the receiver regardless of him being grateful or ungrateful. Rather, something continues to be God’s gifiionly if the person adheres to monotheism and servitude. No one has any position with God and no one is secure from Him except by sheer servitude. That is why He continues to add: and if they had associated others (with Him), certainly what they did would have become ineffectual for them (6:88). He refers to this [ungratefulness and lack of servitude] as shirk (polytheism, association of others with God) because the purpose of the verses is to explain monotheism.

(6:89) Those (ulāʾika) are they to whom We gave the book and the judgment (al-ḥukm) and the prophethood; therefore if these disbelieve in it We have already entrusted with it a people who are not disbelievers in it. The word ulāʾika (those) is a demonstrative pronoun that is used for things at a distance. This indicates the lofty status and exalted position of this group [of prophets and their relatives]. They were given the book, judgment and prophethood in the sense that they as a whole were given these things, not that every single one of them was given all of these. We already explained this in our exposition of the verse: and We chose them and guided them (6:87). In the case of “the book,” it was given only to some of the prophets such as Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus.

When the Qur’an talks about “the book” of the prophets in a general sense [not any specific book], it means a scripture that consists of laws that are used to judge between the people in order to settle their disputes. We can see this meaning in the following verses: (All) people are a single nation; so Allah raised prophets as bearers of good news and as warners, and He revealed with them the Book with truth, that it might judge between people in that in which they differed (2:213); Surely We revealed the Torah in which was guidance and light; with it the prophets who submitted themselves (to Allah) judged (matters).… And We have revealed to you the Book

with the truth, verifying what is before it of the Book and a guardian over it; therefore, judge between them by what Allah has revealed (5:44-48). Ḥukm (judgment, rule) is “to make an affirmative connection between the parts of speech.” One example is when one states that “so-and-so is knowledgeable.” In social affairs and practical matters, both a proposition and the type of relation that it conveys [between the two parts of the sentence] are called ḥukm. Some examples are: “One must do such-and-such

an act”; “It is forbidden to do such-and-such”; “This act is permissible”; “I would like you to do so” and “I would dislike it if you did so.” Therefore, each of the five imperative forms is a ḥukm (judgment, rule)—including wujūb (obligation), ḥurmah (prohibition, being forbidden), jawāz

(permissibility, also called ibāḥah), istiḥbāb (being recommended, being approved) and karāhah (reprehensibility, being disapproved). Likewise, the statements which convey these rules are also called aḥkām (plural of ḥukm). There are also other rules (aḥkām) in societies that are based on other relations such as ownership, management, representation, guardianship, authority and so on.

Ḥukm is also used as an infinitive, meaning “to make and decree a judgment.” This can take several forms:

(1) Legislation and enactment of a law, where a suitable law is set in place to govern the interactions of the people in order to preserve social order.

(2) Exercising personal opinion and issuing a verdict, such as the case of judges and rulers in disputes, where they decide who has the right or who the owner of a property is. Another example is the edicts and rulings issued by those who make legal rulings (sing. fatwá).

(3) Exercising rule over the people, where a ruler or king exercises authority over a territory that is under his rule or possession.

Since the verse mentions ḥukm alongside “the book,” the term is apparently meant in the sense of judgment (qaḍāʾ). Hence, “being given the

book and ḥukm” means that they were given legal rules and the position to judge based on them among the people. This meaning can be clearly seen in many other verses such as: And He revealed with them the Book with truth, that it might judge between people in that in which they differed

(2:213); Surely We revealed the Torah in which was guidance and light; with it the prophets who submitted themselves (to Allah) judged (yaḥkumu)

(5:44); That you may judge (li-taḥkuma) between people by means of that which Allah has taught you (4:105); And David and Solomon when they were giving judgment (yaḥkumāni) concerning the field (21:78); O David! Surely We have made you a ruler in the land; so judge (fa-uḥkum) between men with justice and do not follow desire, lest it should lead you astray from the path of Allah (38:26).

It could also be that ḥukm here has a more general and inclusive meaning [that is, including more than one of the above interpretations], as used

in a verse where Abraham says: My Lord: Grant me judgment (ḥukman), and join me with the righteous (26:83).

We explained the meaning of “prophethood” (nubuwwah) in our exposition of the verse: (All) people were a single nation; so Allah raised prophets (2:213).1 It is a position of receiving news from the unseen through a special divine grace. It pertains to realities that are beyond the visible and sensible world, such God’s unity, the angels and the Last Day. These three qualities by which God blessed the chain of prophets—that is, the book, judgment and prophethood—are mentioned in a thread of verses that serve to describe God’s guidance. Therefore, it can be deduced

It is as if the verses are saying: “The results of that guidance upon which We gathered all prophets and by which We preferred them above all nations were: (1) it led them to a straight path; (2) it made them learn “the book” which comprises of God’s laws; (3) it established them and placed them in a position to judge among the people; and (4) it informed them of unseen realities.

Discussion on the Meaning of “Book” in the Qur’an What comes to our minds nowadays when we hear the word “book”

(kitāb) is a sheet or collection of sheets that convey certain meanings which have been printed or written on them.1 However, the criterion in applying a term is the purpose which it serves, not the particular instance and application to which it was first assigned or which is commonly used today. The purpose of a book is to record certain meanings in a way that one can evoke them by referring to that book. This general definition is not limited to what the hand writes by pen on paper. For example, when one memorizes a book, what the person retains in his memory is also called a “book.” Similarly, when one reads out the book that he has memorized, that is also called a “book,” even though neither of them involves papers or tablets that have been inscribed by pen—as in the case of what we commonly call a “book.”

It is this general and extended meaning of “book” that is used in the Qur’an for what was revealed to the prophets, which is especially used for books that consist of laws and injunctions. The same goes with using the term for something that records the events and occurrences of the universe in one way or another in God’s knowledge. God says: (It is) a Book

We have revealed to you abounding in good (38:29); And We have made every man’s bird of omento cling to his neck, and We will bring forth to him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find wide open:Read your book (17:13-14); No evil befalls on the earth nor in your own souls, but it is in a book before We bring it into existence (57:22). These three verses mark the three usages of “book” in the Qur’an when ascribed to God. The three meanings and usages of “book” in the Qur’an are:

(1) The scriptures which were revealed to the prophets and which

1 Perhaps it can be said that applying “book” to something that has not been written by hand is a generalization of its original meaning. (Auth.) included religious laws, as we said above. God refers to Noah’s book where He says: and He revealed with them the Book with truth (2:213); He refers to the book of Abraham and Moses in the verse: The scriptures of Abraham and Moses (87:19); He mentions the book of Jesus—the Gospel—where He says: And We gave him the Gospel in which was guidance and light (5:46); and He refers to Muḥammad’s book in these verses: These are the verses of the Book and (of) a clear Recitation (15:1), A messenger from Allah, reciting pure pages, Wherein are all the right scriptures (98:2-3), In honored books, exalted, purified; in the hands of scribes: noble, virtuous (80:13-16) and: The Faithful Spirit has descended with itupon your heart, that you may be of the warners, in plain Arabic language (26:193-195).

(2) Books that record the good and evil actions of the people. There are several books in this sense. At the personal level, there are books for each individual, as mentioned in many verses such as: And We have made every man’s omento cling to his neck, and We will bring forth to him on the Day of Resurrection a book (17:13), and The day that every soul shall find present what it has done of good and what it has done of evil (3:30). Then there are books that record the actions of every nation and community, as indicated in the verse: And you shall see every nation kneeling down; every nation shall be called to its book (45:28). Finally, there is a book for all

people, as God says: This is Our book that speaks against you with justice; surely We wrote what you did (45:29), assuming that verse is addressed to all humankind. This sense of book can also be classified according to the classification of the people into good-doers and evil-doers, as He says: Nay! Most surely the record of the wicked is in the Sijjīn. And what will make you know what the Sijjīn is? It is a written book (83:7-9) and then: Nay! Most surely the record of the righteous shall be in the ʿIliyyūn. And what will make you know what the ʿIliyyūn is? It is a written book. Those who are drawn near (to Allah) shall witness it (83:18-21).

(3) Records that incorporate detailed accounts of all events that occur in the universe. There is a book which is secure from all change, where everything is written, as mentioned in these verses: And there does not lie concealed from your Lord the weight of an atom in the earth or in the heaven, nor anything less than that nor greater, but it is in a clear book

(10:61), And We have recorded everything in a clear writing (36:12), And with Us is a writing that preserves (50:4) and: For every term there is a writing (13:38). This also includes the appointed lifetimes that are fixed and unchanging: And a soul will not die but with the permission of Allah, a term fixed (3:145). Perhaps this type of record is divided into a single universal book that includes all events for all beings, and individual books for every being that include the specific conditions of that being. The last two verses [13:38 and 3:145] and other similar verses allude to this idea. There are also records that are subject to change, effacement and establishment, as the Qur’an says: Allah effaces and establishes what He wills, and

with Him is the basis of the Book (13:39). Details of each of these books shall be discussed in its appropriate place in this work, and God is to be sought for help.

The only exception here is how God describes the Torah: And We ordained for him in the tablets admonition of every kind and clear explanation of all things (7:145); And he threw down the tablets and seized his

brother (7:150); And when Moses’ anger calmed down he took up the tablets, and in the writing thereof was guidance and mercy for those who fear for the sake of their Lord (7:154).1

Discussion on the Meaning of “Judgment” in the Qur’an Given its usage, it can be deduced that the root meaning of the term ḥukm (judgment, rule) is manʿ (to stop, to prevent, to restrain). An authoritative or magisterial rule (al-ḥukm al-mawlawī) is called ḥukm because it

prevents the audience from acting and exercising his will unconditionally. It reins the person from doing everything that he wishes.2 A legal verdict is also called ḥukm because it prevents the case from being shaken by quarrel and dispute, and/or because it stops transgression and oppression. Propositions are also called ḥukm because they remove doubt and uncertainty. If something is characterized by iḥkām and istiḥkām (strength,

establishment, robustness) it means that it is in a condition that prevents outside forces and factors from overcoming it or disintegrating its parts. Another sense of iḥkām (concision, compactness, integrity) is the opposite of tafṣīl (differentiation, elaboration). Tafṣīl is to separate something into parts and pieces, which causes the disintegration of its components and

breaks their unity. God says: (This is) a Book, whose verses are made decisive (uḥkimat, from iḥkām); then are they well-elaborated (fuṣṣilat, from tafṣīl), from the All-Wise, the All-Aware (11:1). Muḥkam (decisive, solid, clear) as opposed to mutashābih (ambiguous) also reduces to the same root.1 Al-Rāghib says in al-Mufradāt:

The root of ḥukm is “to prevent and stop for the purpose of improvement and correction.” It is from this root that an animal’s bit is called ḥakamah. One says ḥakamtu and aḥkamtu when one controls an animal by a bit. Aḥkamtuhā means “I made a bit for it [the animal].” Similarly it is said: ḥakamtu or aḥkamtu al-safīh,2 as a poet said: “O children of pure religion! Restrain your fools.” The ḥukm (judgment, rule) of God can have three meanings:

(1) Sometimes it is in matters pertaining to creation (takwīn). In these cases, God’s ḥukm is His existential decree, which is His existentiation of things. That is when He brings something to existence. God’s existential decree and rule (ḥukm) is inseparable from the actual and external existence of that thing at its level of existence.3 He says: And Allah judges; no

one can repel His judgment (13:41); Andwhen He decrees an affair, He only says to it “Be,” so there it is (2:117). The following verse can also be explained

based on this type of divine judgment: Those who were proud shall say: Surely we are all in it; surely Allah has judged between the servants (40:48). (2) Sometimes God’s ḥukm is in legislative matters (tashrīʿ). In these cases, God’s ḥukm refers to His authoritative command and legislation. He says: And they have the Torah wherein is Allah’s judgment (5:43); And who is better than Allah to judge? (5:50).

(3) Sometimes God’s ḥukm refers to God’s fulfilment of His promise and execution of His judgment, as the Qur’an says: And Thy promise is surely true, and Thou art the most just of the judges (11:45).1 When ḥukm is attributed to the prophets, it means “legal judgment. It refers to their position of making judicial decrees, which was given to them by God. The Qur’an says [to Prophet Muḥammad]: Therefore judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their low desires (to turn away) from the truth that has come to you (5:48) and: Those are they to whom We gave the book and the judgment(6:89). Perhaps some verses which talk about “the prophets being given ḥukm” mean—either directly or indirectly—that they were made legislative authorities [that is, they were given the position to make laws.] One example is Abraham’s supplication as narrated in the Qur’an: My Lord: Grant me judgment (ḥukman), and join me with the righteous (26:83).

The Qur’an ascribes two kinds of ḥukm to non-prophets: (1) qaḍāʾ (judgment, according to God’s legislation), as it says: And the followers of the Gospel should have judged by what Allah revealed in it (5:47); (2) tashrīʿ (legislation of new laws regardless of God’s revelation), which is disapproved in the Qur’an: And they set apart a portion for Allah out of what He has created of crops and cattle, and they say: This is for Allah—in their make-believe—and this for our associates… evil is that which they judge (6:136)

… therefore if these (hāʾulāʾ) disbelieve in it (bihā) We have already entrusted with it a people (qawman) who are not disbelievers in it (bihā): The demonstrative pronoun “these” (hāʾulāʾ) refers to those who disbelieved in the Prophet’s call. One group that is certainly among them would

be the disbelievers in Mecca, whom God describes as follows: Surely those who disbelieve, it is alike to them whether you warn them or you do not warn them; they will not believe (2:6).

The pronoun “it” in disbelieve in it and disbelievers in it refers to “guidance” (hudá) [in the last verse: This is Allah’s guidance (6:88)]. Although

hudá is masculine it can be referred to by a feminine pronoun [“it” (hā)

Given the first interpretation of “it,” the meaning would be: “If the polytheists among your people disbelieve in Our guidance—which is Our path—then We have already entrusted this guidance to some of Our servants who do not disbelieve in it.” In this case, the object of belief and disbelief would be guidance, especially guidance in the sense of a path, as the Qur’an narrates [from the jinn]: And that when we heard the guidance (al-hudá), we believed in it (72:13). This sense of guidance is attributed to God and His communications: Then whoever follows My guidance

(hudāya), no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve (2:38). Given the second interpretation of “it,” the verse would mean: “If the polytheists in Mecca disbelieve in the book, the judgment and the prophethood—which define the divine path and the religious call—then We have already entrusted these to a people who do not disbelieve in it.” The word qawman (a people) is in the indefinite form, which shows the significance and lofty status of these “people.” However, exegetes have widely disagreed over who these “people” are. Here is a list of their views followed by our evaluation:

(1) A people in this verse refers to the above-mentioned prophets, which numbered eighteen, or all prophets that are either named personally or described by: And from among their fathers and their descendants

and their brethren (6:87).

Evaluation: The problem with this interpretation is that it contravenes the text of the verse, because who are not disbelievers in it is in the present or present continuous tense. This is while none of the above-mentioned prophets was present when these verses were revealed. If they were meant by the verse, then the verse should have said: “who were not disbelievers in it” [in the past tense]. Nor can one say that “a people” are the prophets including the Messenger of God who was alive at the time. Even though he was one of the prophets—and in fact the highest of them—he is not meant in this verse because he only comes into play in the next verse: These are they whom Allah guided; therefore, follow their guidance (6:90).

1 In Arabic, singular feminine pronouns are also used for plural unintelligent beings. (Trans.)

(2) The verse refers to the angels.

Evaluation: As some exegetes have pointed out, the word qawm (people) is not used for angels, especially when it is used unconditionally

[as in this verse]. It is not a meaning that springs to the mind at first. Moreover, the verse involves a tone of comforting the Prophet, but there is no comfort against the disbelief of his community by saying that the angels believe in him.

(3) A people here refers to those who had believed in the Prophet in Mecca before the revelation of this chapter, or all of the Muhājirīn (Meccan Immigrants).

Evaluation: The problem with this view is that some of those believers later apostatized. God describes one of them later in the chapter as:

he who says: I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed (6:93). Also, some of them were hypocrites. These groups cannot be called a people who are not disbelievers in it.1

(4) The verse refers to the Anṣār (Medinite Supporters), or to both the Muhājirīn and the Anṣār, or to all of the Prophet’s Companions. They were those who uplified the religious call, and who helped the Prophet in his difficult times. They are also has praised very highly elsewhere in the Qur’an.

Evaluation: Even though there is no doubt in the nobility and lofty status of these groups collectively, there was still among them those who turned back after believing, and also hypocrites who were not known at the time. These groups do not match a description such as: We have already entrusted with it a people who are not disbelievers in it (6:89) because this description apparently suggests that these people are completely free from disbelief. Otherwise it should have said: “We have already entrusted with it a people who will believe in it (yuʾminūna bihā)” or “who believed in it (āmanū bihā).”

(5) The verse is talking about the establishment and preservation of belief in a community as a whole, which does not contradict the existence of few individuals among them who are not believers. In other words, who are not disbelievers in it is a description of a group; if a few members of the group do not match this description, it does not entail that the group as a whole cannot have this description. This applies to the believers in

1 Since this is a nominal sentence (ismiyyah, in terms of its Arabic structure),

it suggests continuity of their belief. (Trans.)

the Prophet—such as the Anṣār, or else both them and the Muhājirīn, or else all of his Companions—because belief was firmly established and maintained among them collectively even though it may have dissipated from some of them.

Evaluation: It should be noted that if this view sufficiently explains the verse, then “people” (qawm) would be all Muslims or all believers in all times. It cannot be restricted to only a subgroup of them [who lived at the time of revelation in Mecca and/or Medina]. It is true that some of these people had special religious merits and roles, such as the Muhājirīn being the first to believe in God and endure hardship in His way, or the Anṣār raising the message of monotheism and establishing themselves in the Prophet’s place of migration and in faith [59:9]. However, this only makes the current verse an additional merit for them, but it does not make its description limited to them such that the description does not apply to others who also possess this quality of belief.

Yet, the above view suffers from the following problem: When it comes to describing a community by a quality that does not apply to all of its members, the Qur’an always specifies the exceptions that fall outside that description in one way or another if applicable. For example, God says: Certainly We created humankind in the best make. Then We rendered him to the lowest of the low. Except those who believe (95:4-6); Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are strict against the disbelievers, compassionate among themselves… Allah has promised those among

them who believe and do good, forgiveness and a great reward (48:29);1 Surely the hypocrites are in the lowest stage of the Fire… Except those who repent and amend and hold fast to Allah and are sincere in their religion to Allah (4:145-146); How shall Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their believing… Except those who repent after that and amend (3:86-89). This notion is found frequently throughout the Noble Qur’an. So how is it that the exceptions which fall outside a people who are not disbelievers in it are not mentioned here?

(6) A strange explanation offered by some exegetes is that the verse is about the Anṣār, and what it means by “not being disbelievers in it” is that when these verses were revealed, they had not rejected the Prophet’s call as

exception here because it reduces a universal statement to a particular one. (Trans.)

the Meccan polytheists had, even though they were not yet believers either. Evaluation: There are several problems with this view: (i) It suffers from the same problem that we mentioned about the previous views.1 (ii) At the time of revelation of these verses, the people of Medina—who later became the Anṣār—were polytheists and idolaters. Therefore it is not correct to deny their kufr (disbelief, infidelity)—unless one interprets kufr here as rejecting something after being called to it, which would be an act of defiance and arrogance. However, such an interpretation cannot be granted here because the purpose of these verses is to describe God’s guidance, which is the opposite of associating partners with Him, as He said above: and if they had associated others (with Him), certainly what they did would have become ineffectual for them (6:88). (iii) “Entrustment” in this verse is a means to “preservation and maintenance.” It does not make sense to say that “if these people disbelieve in it, then We shall preserve the message by a people who have neither accepted it nor rejected it.” (7) A people here refers to non-Arabs (al-ʿajam) even though they were not believers at the time.

Evaluation: Apparently this view is taken from the verse: If He will, He can make you pass away, O people, and bring others (4:133) where there are narrations saying that “others” are non-Arabs. However, this view also suffers from the same problems mentioned above.

(8) A people here refers to the believers among Muḥammad’s nation, or believers in all nations.

Evaluation: This view also suffers from the same problems as mentioned above. Yet, it can be amended by saying that the verse is about

certain individuals who believe in God and do not turn back to disbelief as long as they are alive. Such a group can be called “those who believe in this call, who are not disbelievers in it.” Their disbelief remains a possibility, but this possibility never occurs because they persist in their belief,

free from any tinge of disbelief or hypocrisy. Thus they can properly be described as a people who are not disbelievers in it (6:89). This interpretation also confirms the purpose of the verse, which is to console the

Prophet and comfort his noble heart against the disbelief and defiance of the polytheists in response to his call to believe in God and His communications. It also conveys the intended notion of God’s dominance in

preserving His guidance and path with which He honored His chosen servants and prophets.

1 That is the problem of continuity of belief. (Trans.)

However, the above view interprets the verse based on an accidental event, which is that some of those who believe in God’s guidance happen to remain steadfast and not lose their faith, without anything to ensure this. This does not fit the expression, We have already entrusted with it, because entrustment entails trust and reliance, and involves a sense of preservation and maintenance. It does not make sense to take pride and boast in

something when there is no guarantee that it shall persist and continue to function. Moreover, God has criticized many of those who believe by saying: And most of them do not believe in Allah without associating others (with Him) (12:106). This is while the current verses describe a sheer

innate monotheism and a type of divine guidance that is pure and free from any mix of polytheism and iniquity. This [kind of pure belief and guidance] is what God blessed His friend Abraham with, as well as many noble prophets before and after him, as He narrates from Abraham: Those who believe and do not mix up their belief with iniquity, those are they who shall have the security and they are those who have found guidance (6:82). Not all believers can be considered as protectors and trustees from God to preserve this level of guidance from loss and corruption, because among them are certainly transgressors, sinners, pharaohs, tyrants, wrongdoers, innovators, and many who are immersed in iniquity and various forms of indecency and wickedness.

Our interpretation:… therefore if these disbelieve in it We have already entrusted with it a people who are not disbelievers in it: To explain this part of the verse plausibly, we should make note of a two points:

(1) The previous verses described innate monotheism and divine guidance that are free from any mix of associating others with God. They said

that God has bestowed this guidance as a preferential treatment upon a continuous and united chain of prophets, some of them being descendants of others. God has chosen and guided them all to a straight path

that is immune from any error, and has given them the book, judgment and the prophethood.

(2) Then God says, with a tone of pride and glory, while also consoling the Prophet: therefore if these disbelieve in it We have already entrusted

with it a people who are not disbelievers in it. This comforts the Prophet’s soul so that he may not be discouraged by sorrow, and may not lose his determination in making the religious call because of the denial, arrogance and blind transgression of his people.

Given these two points, the meaning would be: “Do not be grieved by what you see of their disbelief in this divine guidance and path which is found in the book, the judgment and the prophethood that We gave to the guided chain of the noble prophets—for indeed We have entrusted this guidance to a people who are not disbelievers in it. As a result, there is no way that this divine guidance may undergo loss and destruction, because We have entrusted this chain with Our guidance and have relied on them to preserve it, and they are certainly not disbelievers in it.”

The disbelief of these “people” [that is, the chain of prophets and saints] is inconceivable, and it is impossible for any tinge of polytheism to enter their hearts, because God has entrusted them with His path and has relied on them to preserve His guidance. If their polytheism and deviation were possible, then relying on them would be a mistake and error, but we know that God “neither errs nor forgets” [20:52].

Thus, the verse shows—and God knows best—that in every time and age God has one or more servants that have been entrusted with the same guidance and path which He gave to His prophets through their books, their judgment and their prophethood. Through them God preserves His religion against loss and His guidance against extinction. Polytheism and iniquity have no way to reach these people because they have clung to God’s protection. These are the infallibles, including the noble prophets and their successors.

Given the above, this verse pertains exclusively to the infallibles. The most one can do in generalizing and extending the verse is to also include righteous believers who are safeguarded against polytheism and iniquity by maintaining taqwá (Godwariness, self-restraint, piety), good deeds and pure faith. They would be those who are out of Satan’s authority, as God says: Surely he has no authority over those who believe and rely on their Lord (16:99). They can also be included in the verse if it can be maintained that God has entrusted them with His guidance and relied on them to preserve it.

(6:90) These are they whom Allah guided, therefore follow (iqtadih, from iqtidāʾ) their guidance. Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it; it is nothing but a reminder (dhikrá) to the nations.

This verse provides another description of the above-mentioned individuals, which were mentioned in order to define God’s special guidance. His guidance certainly does not fail to have its intended impact,

which is to make the person reach the goal [of eternal happiness]. He says: Yet surely Allah does not guide one whom He leads astray (16:37). According to al-Rāghib, dhikrá is more expressive of the meaning of “reminder” than dhikr. The verse also shows the universality of the Prophet’s prophethood for all people.

Iqtidāʾ means ittibāʿ (to follow, to emulate). God orders the Prophet to follow “their guidance” not “themselves.” This is because the Prophet’s shariah (legal code) abrogated theirs, his book overshadows theirs, and the above-mentioned guidance is a kind of guidance that comes without any intermediary between God and the person who is guided. The verse involves an honorary ascription of guidance to “them” by saying their guidance. Otherwise, this guidance is primarily attributable to God, as we read above: This is Allah’s guidance… (6:88).

Based on this verse, some exegetes have inferred that the Prophet and his followers used to practice the ritual and legal codes of the previous prophets except in cases that were specifically abrogated. However, this interpretation would only be plausible had the verse said, “follow them,” but the verse says, “follow their guidance.” Clearly the above interpretation cannot be deduced from this expression.

God then concludes His speech about innate monotheism and divine guidance by addressing His Prophet: Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it; it is nothing but a reminder to the nations (6:90). It is as if the verse

is giving the following commands to the Prophet: (1) Follow the divine guidance which the previous prophets followed. (2) Remind all nations of the divine guidance without asking them for any reward for it. (3) Tell them this to assure their souls, to make your call succeed, and to be farther away from any accusation. God has also narrated this point [that the

prophets do not require any compensation from their nations for their mission] from Noah and the later prophets as part of their call.

Different nations and communities differ in how they define and identify kinship. For example: (1) Are women included in it or not? (2) Do the children of one’s daughter count as his own children? (3) Is kinship only through birth or does it also include iddiʿāʾ (attribution)?1 Arabs during the pre-Islamic era (jāhiliyyah) considered women to only hold “natural” kinship, where they would get married, be provided for by their spouse, and so on. They did not consider women to hold any “legal” kinship where they would be entitled to inheritance and other legal rights. They also did not consider the children of one’s daughter to be part of one’s kin, but they considered attributed children (adʿiyāʾ) to be part of one’s kin. They would use the word ibn (son) for an attributed son. Their practice did not have any lexical basis, but rather they were following the civic laws or tribal customs that were practiced in advanced neighboring nations such as Rome and Persia.

W hen Islam came, it abolished the kinship of attributed children altogether. The Qur’an says: Nor has He made those whom you claim to be your sons your real sons (33:4). Moreover, Islam revised kinship to include women—with its legal implications [such as inheritance]. It also treated the children of one’s daughter to be one’s own children. God says in verses about inheritance: Allah enjoins you concerning your children: the male shall have the equal of the portion of two females (4:11); Men shall have a portion of what the parents and the near relatives leave, and women shall have a portion of what the parents and the near relatives leave, whether there is little or much of it (4:7).

Concerning unlawful marriages, God says: Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters…and lawful for you are (all women) besides those (4:23-24), where He clearly uses daughter for the daughter of one’s daughter.2 God also says: and John and Jesus and Elias (6:85), where God counts Jesus to be a descendant of Abraham or Noah, while he only connects to them through his mother.
